topics.title: Strong passwords vs complex passwords: they're not the same
topics.angle: Most people equate symbols/numbers/uppercase with strength. The real driver of strength is length and unpredictability. Walk through why P@ssw0rd1 is weak and a random four-word phrase is strong, without using entropy math.
topics.audience: Anyone with online accounts who's been confused by password complexity rules

topics.title: The one password habit that quietly hurts most people
topics.angle: Reusing a password across sites is the highest-impact common mistake. When one site is breached, attackers try those credentials everywhere (credential stuffing). Explain in plain terms, give the practical fix.
topics.audience: General readers who reuse passwords because remembering many is hard

topics.title: How to spot a phishing login page before you type
topics.angle: Concrete cues: domain check, padlock isn't enough, hover-before-click, urgency-as-red-flag. Make the reader confident at recognizing the 80% common case, honest about the harder ones.
topics.audience: General readers who get sketchy emails and want to handle them better

topics.title: Two-factor authentication, explained without jargon
topics.angle: What 2FA actually is, the three common kinds (SMS code, authenticator app, hardware key), where each fits, and why SMS is the weakest of the three. Avoid implying SMS is useless — it's still better than nothing.
topics.audience: Readers who've seen '2FA' in account settings and never turned it on

topics.title: Your password was in a breach. Here's what actually matters next
topics.angle: Most breach-response advice is generic panic. The real priority order: change the password on the breached site first, then anywhere else you reused it, then enable 2FA. What is and isn't worth doing.
topics.audience: Anyone who got a 'your data was exposed' notification

topics.title: What a password manager actually does (and doesn't do)
topics.angle: Demystify password managers for someone who's never used one. What they store, what they don't, what 'master password' means, what happens if you forget it. Mention VaultMesh once here as an example of a local-first option (per STYLE.md rules).
topics.audience: People considering using a password manager for the first time

topics.title: Why 'security questions' are often the weakest link
topics.angle: Mother's maiden name, first pet, etc. — most of these are findable on social media. Why they exist anyway, and what to do when a site insists on them (lying / using a manager-generated answer).
topics.audience: Anyone who's filled out a security question form

topics.title: Public WiFi: what's a real risk, and what isn't anymore
topics.angle: HTTPS-everywhere has made the old 'man in the middle on coffee shop WiFi' threat much smaller. What still matters (fake captive portals, untrusted networks for sensitive admin work), what doesn't.
topics.audience: Travelers and remote workers who worry about hotel/cafe WiFi

topics.title: Browser-saved passwords: convenient, but at what cost?
topics.angle: The trade-offs of letting Chrome / Safari / Firefox remember your passwords. Where they're stored, how they sync, when this is fine, when it isn't.
topics.audience: Anyone who clicked 'Save password' in their browser

topics.title: Four random words: the passphrase that's stronger than it looks
topics.angle: Walk through why a randomly-chosen 4-word phrase (e.g., the EFF diceware list) is both memorable and resistant to guessing — and why deliberately picking 4 words yourself doesn't count as random.
topics.audience: Readers who want one strong master password they can actually remember

topics.title: Why your email account deserves more protection than anything else
topics.angle: Your email is the recovery address for every other account you own. Whoever controls your inbox can reset your bank, your work login, your everything. This single account warrants extra protection — a strong unique password and 2FA at minimum.
topics.audience: Anyone who has multiple online accounts and hasn't thought of email as a central point of failure

topics.title: You don't need to change your password every 90 days
topics.angle: The 'change passwords regularly' rule is outdated and counterproductive — it leads to weaker passwords, not stronger ones. NIST guidance since 2017 says to change passwords when compromised, not on a schedule. Explain why, and clarify when you actually should change a password.
topics.audience: Anyone whose workplace or bank still enforces periodic password changes

topics.title: The account settings most people never update
topics.angle: Recovery email and recovery phone number are the real keys to your accounts — but most people set them once and forget. Old email addresses, disconnected phone numbers, ex-employers' emails. What to audit and why it matters.
topics.audience: Anyone who has had the same accounts for years without reviewing recovery settings

topics.title: SIM swapping: when someone steals your phone number
topics.angle: SIM swap attacks let an attacker take over your phone number by convincing your carrier to transfer it. Once they have your number, SMS-based 2FA is theirs. Explain how it works, who's at risk, and the practical steps to reduce exposure (carrier PIN, move away from SMS 2FA for high-value accounts).
topics.audience: Anyone who uses SMS codes for two-factor authentication

topics.title: Staying logged in: when it's fine and when it isn't
topics.angle: The 'remember me' checkbox and persistent login sessions are convenient but not always appropriate. Explain what a session actually is, what risks come from staying logged in on shared or lost devices, and the simple habit that mitigates most of it (lock your device).
topics.audience: Anyone who clicks 'remember me' without thinking about it

topics.title: How to share account access without sharing a password
topics.angle: Sharing passwords by text or email is common but risky. Cover the better options: services that have built-in sharing or family plans, password manager sharing features, and why the credential itself shouldn't travel over chat. Practical for both families and small teams.
topics.audience: Anyone who has sent a password over text, email, or Slack

topics.title: Passkeys: the sign-in method that doesn't use a password
topics.angle: Passkeys are now supported by Apple, Google, and Microsoft. Explain what they are (a cryptographic key pair tied to your device, no password to steal or phish), how they work without being technical, and what to do when a site offers one. Honest about the current limitation: they don't yet work everywhere.
topics.audience: Anyone who has seen 'Sign in with a passkey' and wasn't sure what to make of it

topics.title: What 'Sign in with Google' actually does to your account
topics.angle: OAuth social login is convenient but creates a dependency: if your Google or Apple account is compromised, so is everything connected to it. Explain what's actually being shared, when social login is a reasonable choice, and when a standalone login is worth the extra step.
topics.audience: Anyone who routinely clicks 'Continue with Google' without thinking about what that means

topics.title: Not all data breaches are the same
topics.angle: When a breach notice arrives, the urgency depends on what was actually exposed. Explain the difference between plaintext passwords (change immediately), hashed passwords (change soon, monitor), and metadata-only breaches (lower urgency) — without entropy math or crypto jargon.
topics.audience: Anyone who gets breach notifications and doesn't know how seriously to take them

topics.title: Backup codes: the 2FA safety net most people never save
topics.angle: When you enable 2FA, most services offer one-time backup codes for account recovery. Most people skip saving them and later get locked out when they lose their phone or switch authenticator apps. Explain what backup codes are, why they matter, and where to store them safely.
topics.audience: Anyone who has set up 2FA but didn't save the backup codes — or doesn't know what they are

topics.title: The apps still connected to your accounts
topics.angle: When you use 'Sign in with Google' or connect a tool to your account, it retains ongoing access — often long after you've stopped using it. Old, forgotten apps with account access are a real risk. Walk through how to find and revoke them on major platforms.
topics.audience: Anyone who has connected apps or services to their Google, Apple, or Microsoft account and never reviewed them

topics.title: Phishing by text: how SMS scams work and how to spot them
topics.angle: Smishing (SMS phishing) follows the same formula as email phishing but feels more personal. Fake delivery notifications, bank alerts, and government texts are the most common formats. Walk through the tells and the same core rule: don't tap a link in an unsolicited text — go directly to the site.
topics.audience: Anyone who gets unexpected texts from banks, couriers, or government agencies

topics.title: How to find and fix your weakest passwords
topics.angle: Most people have a handful of genuinely risky passwords mixed in with fine ones. Explain how to do a practical audit: check HaveIBeenPwned, use a password manager's built-in audit feature if available, and prioritize which to fix first (email and banking before everything else).
topics.audience: Anyone who suspects they have some weak or reused passwords but doesn't know where to start

topics.title: Device encryption: why it matters when your phone goes missing
topics.angle: Full-device encryption means that a thief who gets your phone can't read its contents without your PIN. Most modern phones enable it by default, but many people don't know it's there or whether it's on. Explain what it does, how to verify it's enabled, and why the lock screen PIN is more important than it looks.
topics.audience: Anyone who stores passwords, photos, or sensitive data on a phone or laptop
